E0095.summary: Author whose accounts of initiation into the mysteries of Isis Atwood uses repeatedly to illustrate the inner light, the goddess (Universal Nature) and the soul's liberation.
E0095.body:
Atwood cites Apuleius chiefly as a witness of initiation. From *On the God of Socrates* she takes the inner light experienced when separated from the body: “this knowledge sometimes shines forth with a most rapid coruscation like a bright and clear light in the most profound darkness” [II.3 ¶50, II.3 n54]; his 'midnight Sun' she identifies with the ignited Stone [II.3 ¶54]. The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) likewise uses the midnight sun seen when initiated by Isis to illustrate the coruscation of released light [APP ¶126].

From the *Metamorphoses*, book 11, she draws: the bough connected with the Mercurial caduceus in the procession of Isis initiates [II.3 ¶11, II.3 n6]; the appearance of the goddess (Isis/nature) in the Eleusian Fane and her mandates to the initiate — “Moved by thy prayers, O Lucius! Behold, I am come!” [II.4 ¶16, II.4 ¶17, II.4 n9]; Lucius' praise of the goddess, which Atwood applies to the Universal Nature — “Thou rollest the heavens round the steady poles, dost illuminate the sun, govern the world, and tread on the dark realms of Tartarus.” [II.4 ¶18, II.4 n10]; and Lucius' rosy crown and shedding of the beast's hide as images of the soul's liberation [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n11].

He is listed with Plotinus, Philo-Judaeus, Proclus, Porphyry, Jamblicus and Julian among the Alexandrian revival figures professing Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27]; he is called to witness by Agrippa [II.1 ¶26]; and Reuchlin's passage cites him to excuse an obscure phrase: “you must pardon, as Apuleius says, the strange expression” [III.2 ¶24]. In I.1 ¶11 he appears as the hypothetical forger of the prophecy, a theory Atwood rejects.

E0096.summary: Author of the Metapmorphoses, or Golden Ass, cited for being turned into an ass before admission to the mysteries of Isis.
E0096.body: Atwood cites the *Metapmorphoses, or Golden Ass* of Apuleius of Megara to illustrate that he was turned into an ass before his admission to the mysteries of Isis [III.2 ¶64, III.2 n47].

E0097.summary: Treatise in the Mus. Herm. cited for verses on the regeneration (union, dissolution, reunion of spirit, soul and body) and for the triune universal essence.
E0097.body:
Atwood quotes translated verses from the *Aquarium Sapientum* (in Mus. Herm., 'The Enigma'): spirit, soul and body in one seat, then dissolution, then reunion in the last heat — “The Spirit is given to the body for a time,” [III.1 ¶51, III.1 ¶52, III.1 n57]. She endorses this as 'the constant doctrine and rule of the regeneration'.

Under the spelling *Aquarium Sepientum* (Mus. Herm., p. 112) it is cited after the birth of Horus to illustrate the triune and fivefold divine-human essence: “Triuna universalis essentia, quae Jehovah appellatur” [IV.2 ¶11, IV.2 n3].

E0098.summary: Apparently a region that consciousness must pass through, clear and rational, before entering the Fire World; the text does not define it further.
E0098.body: Atwood speaks of consciousness passing “clear and rational from out the Aquaster, enters the Fire World” [II.3 ¶16]; a quoted adept likewise speaks of “he that has once passed the Aquaster, and entered the Fire World” [II.3 ¶41]. The context suggests a middle region traversed before the Fire World, but the text gives no definition.

E0099.summary: Confessed adept whose alchemical treatises Atwood cites for transmutation, deliberate obscurity, secrecy and the sufficiency of Mercury, while criticizing his 'false panegyrists'.
E0099.body:
Atwood cites Aquinas (Thesaurus Alchimiae, addressed to brother Reinaldo; Meteorum, lib. iv; De Esse et Essentia; Secreta Alchimiae) as a confessed adept affirming transmutation — “Metalla transmutari possunt unum in aliud” [I.1 ¶39, I.1 n49] — and for his deliberate obscurity and warnings to keep the secret from worldly seekers, which she takes to point to the art's higher theosophical purpose [I.1 ¶41, I.1 ¶42, I.1 n50, I.1 n51]. She criticizes his 'false panegyrists'.

From the *Roasrium Abbrev.* (Tract. iii and v) she takes the doctrine that Mercury alone suffices, being the root of gold and silver and working itself: “It is Mercury alone which perfects in our work” [I.2 ¶11, I.2 n13].

E0100.summary: An Arabian authority (given in the Rosarium as Aristotele Arabus) cited on the Stone: nothing is added, separation only removes superfluities.
E0100.body: Via the *Rosarium* (Aristotele Arabus), 'the Arabian' supports the claim that nothing is added in the work: “to which we add nothing different or extract, only in the separation removing superfluities” [I.2 ¶43, I.2 n42]. His 'subtle phrase' on the Stone known and proven is also cited: “Sumatur lais in capitulis notus” [III.2 ¶7].

E0101.summary: Apparently a place or vessel in which the two serpents, tied in a love knot, are shut up; the text does not explain it.
E0101.body: In a passage from Cornelius Agrippa's 'ingenious disciple', the two serpents are to be bound and enclosed: “tie them in a love knot and shut them up in the Arabian Caraha” [III.1 ¶50]. The context suggests a vessel or enclosure, but the text gives no explanation.

E0102.summary: In Vaughan's account, the philosophers' medicine reduced by bodily fermentation to a portable dust.
E0102.body: Quoting Vaughan, Atwood records that the philosophers reduced their medicine by bodily fermentation to a dust: “they reduced their medicine to a dust, and this dust is the Arabian Elixir” [IV.3 ¶22] — so the Arabian Elixir = this dust. Unlike the medicine itself it was portable: “This Elixir the philosophers could carry about them” [IV.3 ¶22].

E0103.summary: Cited to characterize the 'entertaining' style of the Christian philosophers' promises.
E0103.body: Atwood invokes the *Arabian Nights* to illustrate the 'entertaining' style of the Christian philosophers' promises [II.3 ¶34].

E0104.summary: Group voice cited for a name of the Matter: Flower of White Salt.
E0104.body: The Arabians are cited for a name of the Matter: “Flos Salis Albi” (Flower of White Salt) [III.2 ¶8].

E0105.summary: Cited within a Vaughan passage to show that the work does not occupy the operator's attention.
E0105.body: In a passage from Vaughan, the *Arcadia* illustrates that the work does not occupy the attention: “a lady may read the Arcadia” [III.4 ¶38].

E0106.summary: The secret of the work: the 'great Arcanum' possessed when the tincture rises from the black, identified by Albertus with 'our brass', and wholly revealed to Eirenaeus.
E0106.body:
The term appears mostly in quoted voices. A 'more modern experimentalist' says that when the masculine tincture rises from the black “he will then know that he hath the great Arcanum of the world” [I.3 n53]. Albertus (spelled 'Mangus') identifies the 'occult Arcanum' with 'our brass', to be washed until pure: “Take, says Albertus Mangus, the occult Arcanum, which is our brass, and wash it that it may be pure and clean” [II.2 ¶16]. Urbigeranus and other Adepts make the Theory of their Arcanum the medium by which the Royal Diadem is extracted; without it dissolution is impossible: “it will be entirely impossible to accomplish without the Theory of their Arcanum” [IV.1 ¶7].

Atwood herself uses it for the whole secret of the work, revealed to Eirenaeus in two and a half years: “the whole Arcanum was revealed to him” [IV.1 ¶17]. In the plural, Eirenaeus speaks of the Chaos “in which all the Arcana are contained; not in act as yet, but in virtue” [IV.1 ¶43] — the secrets present potentially, not yet actually.

E0107.summary: Work supplying the epigraph of IV.1, setting the theme that the arts are bought by labor.
E0107.body: The chapter epigraph of IV.1 comes from *Arcanum Ignis Aquae* (Resp. 6): “Dii sudoribus vendunt Artes” [IV.1 ¶1] — the gods sell the arts for sweat (translation ours), setting the theme of labor.

E0108.summary: Work cited for a Latin statement on transmuting the salt of blood by urinous ferment.
E0108.body: Atwood cites the *Arcanum Liquaris Alkahest* (Resp. 876, 78) in Latin on transmuting the salt of blood: “sanquinis salem per urinaceum fermentum sic transmutari debere” [II.1 ¶21, II.1 n18] — that the salt of blood ought thus to be transmuted by a urinous ferment (translation ours).

E0109.summary: Paracelsus' term, which Atwood sets beside the solar plexus as the workshop of the Celestial life, in which the Light lies hidden until drawn out.
E0109.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the term in apposition to the solar plexus: “the solar plexus, the Archaeus of Paracelsus, is its workshop” [APP ¶32] — the workshop of the Celestial life; so Archaeus = solar plexus there. In the main text she speaks of “the Light, so long hidden and enshrined in the Archaeus” [III.3 ¶71], drawn out by artificial heat and exhalation. Van Helmont, quoted, gives the Archaeus a 'sky' in which ideas from the soul's starry heaven and the spirit of the seven bowels are read: “For in the sky of our Archaeus, aspectual Ideas are deciphered” [III.2 ¶17]. The text does not define the term further.

E0110.summary: The order in which all things are causally ranged as originally distributed, seen 'as in a glass' by one who has the Principle.
E0110.body: Atwood speaks of “the great Archetypal Law of Light, in which are all things causally ranged” [III.3 ¶39]: the order of things as originally distributed, which the one who possesses the Principle beholds 'as in a glass'. See also Archetype, whose creative mind orders all things by this Law.

E0111.summary: The original Light before which the understanding stands to perfect its new-born attributes; perceived, it burns up prior images and is identified with Truth.
E0111.body: In the main text, Atwood describes “the understanding vehicle now standing in open presence before its Archetypal Light” [II.4 ¶16], by which it perfects its new-born attributes. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she says that this light, once perceived, burns up all prior images, perceives itself alone, “transmuting all that is not combustible into itself” [APP ¶106]; it is both objective and subjective and is identified with Truth: “for it is objective and subjective both; it is Truth” [APP ¶106].

E0112.summary: The hidden essence of the Intellectual Law, of which ordinary reason is only an embryo image.
E0112.body: Atwood speaks of “that Archetypal Wisdom which the ancients celebrated as the occult essence of that Law” [II.1 ¶35] — the Intellectual Law, of which ordinary reason gives only an embryo image. Archetypal Wisdom = the occult essence of the Intellectual Law.

E0113.summary: The original of which the self and natural things are images; the creative mind ordering all things causally and the end of the soul's progression.
E0113.body:
For Atwood the Archetype is the original of which the self is an image and the end of the soul's progression; it is the creative mind whose Law of Light orders all things causally, “where the Archetype shadows the intellectual spheres” [III.3 ¶39], and in which things are “that which is in the Archetypal mind creatively efficient” [III.3 n27]. In the plural, the Archetypes are the originals of things beheld in nature, which do not truly resemble them: “If indeed things beheld in nature were such as the Archetypes, whence they are derived” [III.2 ¶61]; one established in Intellect is “able through it, as an image, to behold the Archetype” [III.2 ¶66].

In Hermes' account, Poemander asks: “hast thou seen that Archetypal Form, which was before the interminated and infinite beginning?” [III.3 ¶56] — the pattern in which God's Will and Counsel beheld the beautiful world and which it imitated in making this world.

E0114.summary: Pythagorean whose fragments Atwood cites on Wisdom as contemplation of first Principles and on right method of investigation as the key to discovery.
E0114.body: From a fragment given by Taylor in his Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagorus, Archytas supports Atwood's account of Wisdom, which contemplates the whole and discovers the Principles of Being, leading to a vision of Divinity: “he will have conjoined ends with beginnings” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n34]. He also supports her stress on method — mankind has not known how to investigate: “If you investigate rightly, says Archytas, discovery will be easy for you” [II.1 ¶52, II.1 ¶53].

E0115.summary: The philosophic Mercury, the subject of the Art: a water of another nature, a stone and no stone, gold essential but unripe, cleansed and coagulated by its own sulfur.
E0115.body:
The term comes almost entirely in quoted voices. Lully calls it a water of another nature: “argentums vivum nostrum est aqua alterius naturae” [I.2 ¶18]; in it the conversion of natures is carried out: “the method of conversion in our Argent vive is the reduction of natures to their first root” [I.2 ¶25]. Arnold: “it is a stone and no stone, in which the whole Art consists, spirit, soul and body” [I.2 ¶29] — volatile, clear, One Thing.

It is identified with the philosophic Mercury (Hermes and the Scholiast): “for that is Mercury which is spoken of concerning the residual earth” [I.3 ¶9]; “this argent vive, then, which is the residuum of the philosophic earth after the separation” [I.3 n9]. Hermes requires two to be mortified together — “it behooves us to mortify two Argent vives together” [I.3 ¶32]; “the Argent vive of Auripigment and the Oriental Argent vive of magnesia” [III.1 ¶43] — not further explained. Eirenaeus: “For Argent Vive is gold essential Only unripe” [III.1 ¶69], which prepared by art gives the secret menstrual.

The Adept, with Atwood, describes its course: “this Argent vive was at first gross, unclean, fugitive, being mingled with extraneous Sulfurs” [IV.1 ¶10]; cleansed by Art and coagulated by its own internal sulfur, red and white, it becomes subtle and penetrative, resolving mineral bodies; “this Argent vive, which is decocted linearly, is generated pontically” [IV.1 ¶11]. In Geber's definition it is the volatile: “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, that is to say, of the volatile and the fixed” [IV.3 ¶9]. In Eirenaeus' projection verse, “Then upon Argent vive cast this with care.” [IV.3 ¶25] — apparently in the place of the 'mercury purged and purified' of ¶20, though the text does not state this. Vaughan mentions “three Argent vives and as many Salts” [IV.2 ¶35], unexplained.

E0116.summary: Classical allusion used to say the philosophic vessels 'speak for themselves'.
E0116.body: Atwood illustrates that the philosophic vessels speak for themselves: they, “like the planks of Argo, on occasion, are still oracular” [III.4 ¶32].

E0118.summary: Author whose chorus of the Initiated Atwood cites for the privileged light of those who perform acts of piety and justice.
E0118.body: From *In Ramis*, Act 1, Atwood cites the chorus to illustrate the privileged light of the initiated, who perform acts of piety and justice: “The sun shines but for us, exclaims the chorus of the Initiated in Aristophanes” [II.4 ¶16, II.4 n7].

E0119.summary: Authority (the Stagyrite) cited widely on Wisdom, Intellect, Matter and reduction of metals; Atwood qualifies charges of envy against him but declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher.
E0119.body:
Norton and the adepts criticize Aristotle for envy and veiling; Atwood qualifies this, cites his works (epistles to Alexander on the Philosophers' stone, Secreta Secretorum, book of Meteors) as evidence of hidden knowledge, yet declines to call him a Hermetic philosopher without more evidence [I.1 ¶15, I.1 ¶16, I.1 ¶17, I.1 n22]. Through Ripley's verse the *Book of Meteors* concurs that metals are not transmutable unless reduced to their beginning [I.2 ¶5, I.2 ¶6, I.2 n6]; he is cited (n38) for metals reducible to water [III.2 n38].

On Wisdom and Intellect: Wisdom is the highest science, drawn from what is universal in oneself [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n30], the true being of Intellect, small in bulk but surpassing in energy [II.1 n31]; mystical exercises bring the understanding into contact with its cause, and intellect is identical with the intelligible — “True Intellect, he says, is that which is essentially the most essential of that which is most essential” [II.1 ¶37, II.1 n32; cf. II.1 ¶44]. He compares Universals to colors needing the sun and calls human reason 'intellect in capacity' [II.1 ¶34]; his 'passive intellect' names the Mundane Spirit first revealed in humanity [II.2 ¶17]; “That Intellect must be assumed which is most perfectly purified” [III.1 ¶23, III.1 n30]. The self-perceiving final object “is good, according to the words of the Stagyrite, and the end of spiritual generation” [IV.2 ¶8].

On Matter, 'the logician': “I mean, he says, by Matter, that which of itself is neither essence nor quantity” [III.2 ¶53, III.2 n42]. His triple distinction of heaven [III.2 ¶33, III.2 n32] and his 'perfect world', read as the ethereal [III.2 ¶38]; his abstruse diction illustrates concealment; his criticisms of predecessors — “Parmenides appears to have touched upon the One according to Reason; but Melissus, according to Matter” [III.2 ¶38] — are said to aim at the letter, not the spirit, though he is also blamed for making away with his brethren 'after the manner of the Ottomans' [III.2 ¶36]; his logic is praised in its original intent, later degraded [III.2 ¶40, III.2 ¶41, III.2 ¶42, III.2 n37]. From the Ethics: “Ab actionibus procedit speculatio” [IV.1 ¶18]; one deliberates about means, not ends, analyzing back to the first Cause as in a diagram [IV.1 ¶30, IV.1 n25]. 'The Aristotle' is cited for the change of the corruptible into incorruption: “Behold I show you a mystery, says the Aristotle, we shall not all sleep, but we shall be changed” [III.3 ¶27, III.3 n18].

E0120.summary: Ancient rites which, Atwood says, refer to the physical secret of regeneration, the god dead and revived being principal in them.
E0120.body: Atwood states that “the Arkite Mysteries have reference to the physical secret of the regeneration” [III.3 ¶69]; the god dead and revived is principal in them.

E0121.summary: Cited as rites referring to the physical secret of regeneration.
E0121.body: Cited by Atwood in support of the claim that these mysteries refer to the physical secret of regeneration [III.3 ¶69]. See the term entry Arkite Mysteries.

E0122.summary: Something rectified by Power and Motive 'by an infallible rule'; the text does not explain it.
E0122.body: Atwood speaks of Power and Motive that “rectifies the Armed Magnet by an infallible rule” [IV.1 ¶33]. The expression is not explained.

E0123.summary: Mystic named in the Appendix as the one who recognizes the depth of the Psalms.
E0123.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Arndt is named as the one Mystic who recognizes the depth of the Psalms [APP ¶97].

E0124.summary: Confessed adept whose Speculum and Rosarium Atwood cites constantly: reduction to first root, the matter as stone and no stone, dissolution of the Stone in its own mercury.
E0124.body:
Atwood ranks Arnold di Villa Nova as a confessed adept whose skill, including projections with transmuting powder, is attested by contemporaries [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶43]; he possibly convinced Lully by exhibiting transmutation [I.1 ¶48], though Lully did not receive the mystery from him [IV.1 ¶36]. His *Speculum* gives the basis of the whole theory: “there abides in nature a certain pure matter” [I.2 ¶2]; species are indestructible — “Species non transmutari sed individual specierum” [I.2 ¶5, I.2 n3, I.2 n4] — so the subject must be freed by artificial reduction.

His precept “Converte elementa et quod quaeris invenies” [I.2 ¶22] means reduction of natures to their first root [I.2 ¶25]; Atwood glosses “Convert the elements, says Arnold, and you shall have what you desire” as separating and rejoining in harmonious proportion [I.3 n23]. The matter is a stone and no stone: “Ii is a stone and no stone, spirit, soul, and body” [I.3 n5, I.3 n13, I.3 n17], following whatever is done to it [cf. I.2 ¶29, I.2 n30]. From the *Rosarium*: “The work of philosophers, says Arnold, is to dissolve the Stone in its own mercury” [IV.1 ¶7, IV.1 n6], to first Matter; the operator needs “three requisites, viz., subtlety of mind, manual skill, and a free will for the operation” [III.4 ¶20, III.4 n19].

With Hermes he witnesses that the art must be entrusted by one to another [II.1 ¶25]; verse (versifier not named) cites the Rosary of 'Arnolde of the New Towne' for the claim that none can operate alone: “There may noe man Mercury mortify, But it be with his brother’s knowledging.” [I.3 n17]. He is also cited for the same testimony [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n100], as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n25], with Albert and Raymond in Ripley's verse as writing plainly of gold reduced to mineral water [III.1 ¶62], with Lully and Artephius as agreeing with the Lucerna Salis on whitening [III.2 ¶5], and within the Ordinal, where the Art belongs to great men so poor men should beware, and the operator should be patient and gentle: “Esto longanimus et suavis” [IV.1 ¶12].

E0125.summary: The addressee's term for what Nature wraps herself in to realize her imaginings (Appendix).
E0125.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood uses the term as the addressee's own ('what you call'): “She wraps herself about with what you call aromal essences, aromal emanations” [APP ¶122] — Nature clothing herself to realize her imaginings.
